issues.legal_issue: Internal administrative recommendations do not create an enforceable right to an allotment unless the competent final authority approves a decision and it is communicated to the affected person.
material_facts: The technical committee recommended relocation of the two outlets, and other internal steps were taken to consider alternative sites.
The recommendations were not approved as a final decision communicated to the outlet owners; the competent authority later rejected relocation.
issues.conclusion: The recommendations and internal file notings did not create an enforceable right to relocation or bind the development authority.
issues.legal_principle: Internal notings express officials’ opinions for departmental consideration and become an executable decision affecting rights only when approved by the final decision-making authority and communicated to the affected person. In Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab, applying Article 166(1) of the Constitution, the Court held that an uncommunicated ministerial opinion is not an order of the Government; Laxminarayan R. Bhattad v. State of Maharashtra likewise holds that a right created by a statutory authority’s order must be communicated to be enforceable.

rule.if: administrative_allotment_claim and internal_recommendation_made and not final_decision_communicated

predicates.administrative_allotment_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim for an administrative allotment or relocation.
predicates.internal_recommendation_made: Officials or a committee within the authority recommended the requested allotment or relocation.
predicates.final_decision_communicated: The competent final authority approved a decision on the request and communicated it to the affected person.

issues.definition: When an allotment claim rests on an internal recommendation that was not followed by an approved and communicated final decision, the claim does not establish an enforceable allotment right.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant has no enforceable legitimate expectation of relocation where the earlier policy only allowed the request to be considered, the final decision was made after a changed policy took effect, and the request did not meet the revised criteria.
material_facts: The earlier policy allowed relocation requests to be entertained when an oil company or ministry referred a case involving reduced sales and an outlet that was not feasible at its existing location; it did not require the authority to grant relocation.
The outlet owners’ sites had been allotted by another agency, and the proposed road project was expected to reduce access and sales rather than directly require the sites to be closed.

Before the authority’s final decision, a revised policy limited relocation to cases where a planned project directly necessitated closure of the existing site; the authority rejected the requests under the revised policy.
The revised policy was not challenged, and the Court considered it to have been adopted in the public interest; the authority’s decision was not shown to be arbitrary or unreasonable.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of legitimate expectation did not require the authority to relocate the outlets, and the refusal of relocation did not warrant judicial interference.
issues.legal_principle: Legitimate expectation may arise from a representation, past practice, or conduct, but a claimant must establish reliance and detriment; the expectation is a relevant consideration, not by itself an enforceable right. Under Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries and Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation, denial may be reviewed where it is arbitrary, discriminatory, unfair, an abuse of power, or contrary to natural justice, but the doctrine does not displace a fair decision made in the public interest. A policy change may defeat a substantive expectation if it is reasonable, as explained in Punjab Communications Ltd. v. Union of India and Bannari Amman Sugars Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer. The Court also relied on Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service, Attorney General of Hong Kong v. Ng Yuen Shiu, National Buildings Construction Corporation v. S. Raghunathan, Jitendra Kumar v. State of Haryana, and Attorney General for New South Wales v. Quinn. The 1999 and 2003 policies were relevant to whether relocation could be expected; the revised policy was not shown to violate Article 14.

rule.if: administrative_relocation_claim and earlier_policy_only_permitted_consideration and final_decision_after_policy_change and revised_criteria_not_met and policy_change_public_interest_and_unchallenged

predicates.administrative_relocation_claim: The proceeding concerns a claimant seeking relocation of an existing commercial outlet by a public authority.
predicates.earlier_policy_only_permitted_considerat: The earlier policy allowed the authority to consider relocation requests but did not require it to grant them.
predicates.final_decision_after_policy_change: The authority made its final decision after a revised policy had taken effect.
predicates.revised_criteria_not_met: The claimant’s circumstances did not satisfy the revised policy’s conditions for relocation.
predicates.policy_change_public_interest_and_unchal: The revised policy was treated as serving the public interest and was not challenged in the proceeding.

issues.definition: Where an earlier policy only allowed consideration, the final decision followed a public-interest policy change, and the claimant did not meet the revised criteria, the claimant has no enforceable expectation of relocation.
